title: Artificial Intelligence in Federal Courts: A Random-Sample Survey of Judges
pub: The Sedona Conference Journal, Vol. 27 (forthcoming 2026), with the NYC Bar Association Presidential Task Force on AI and Digital Technologies
author: Anika Jaitley · Daniel W. Linna Jr. · Xavier Rodriguez · V.S. Subrahmanian · Siyu Tao

st.t: Professional governance: Existing duties need active AI scrutiny
st.an: The source documents institutional support, multidisciplinary participation and the judiciary subcommittee’s broad remit, but provides no survey findings, governance recommendations or substantive position on whether existing professional duties require active AI scrutiny. Its organizational context is compatible with the cluster but insufficient to establish support or opposition.
qs: The primary mission of the Task Force is to create a Center of Excellence and Thought Leadership in artificial intelligence and digital technologies,

The primary mission of the AI Judiciary Subcommittee includes addressing state and local courts; federal courts; litigants; court administration; specialized technology courts such as artificial intelligence courts and robo judges; and alternative dispute resolution.

st.t: Court responsibility: AI requires lifecycle supervision
st.an: The survey accepts the cluster’s core framing of AI as bounded assistance requiring human verification and institutional oversight, and materially extends it with empirical evidence that federal judges report uneven chambers policies, limited training access, false-citation concerns and demand for clearer safeguards. Its findings support lifecycle supervision without claiming measured model error rates or proven court-wide benefits.
qs: o   Concerned to the extent individuals do not thoroughly check case             cites, facts and holdings.
There is a real need for clear            guidelines, training and oversight.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s supervised, task-bounded framing and materially extends it with random-sample evidence from federal judges: adoption is broad but generally infrequent and research-led, while judges emphasize verification, independent record review, training and risks of hallucination and skill atrophy. Its efficiency claims are mainly respondent expectations rather than measured productivity outcomes.
qs: AI adoption is broad but infrequent: More than 60% of responding judges reported using at least one AI tool in their judicial work.
o AI should always be seen as at most a research aid, and its results            must always be veriﬁed.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The study accepts the cluster’s selective-deployment framing and materially extends it with random-sample evidence from federal judicial chambers. It shows AI concentrated in bounded research and document tasks, limited use for decision-making, and governance organised around use-specific restrictions, verification, confidentiality and training rather than blanket adoption or prohibition. Its sampling and measurement limitations qualify generalisability but do not reverse that alignment.
qs: These responses indicate that many judges are not thinking about AI in binary “yes” or “no” terms but instead are evaluating the beneﬁts and risks of speciﬁc AI use cases.

Several judges clariﬁed that, while AI use is (i) permitted and encouraged or (ii) permitted, even so, certain use cases are not permitted, and permitted uses can be subject to detailed guidelines (such as a requirement to independently verify AI outputs).

st.t: AI adoption: Enthusiasm cannot establish investment value
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s bounded, implementation-focused account: judicial experimentation is broad but routine use is limited, while uneven training and governance, reliability risks, verification requirements and survey limitations prevent enthusiasm or adoption from establishing investment value or autonomous readiness.
qs: However, only 22.4% reported using these tools on a weekly or daily basis.
o AI should always be seen as at most a research aid, and its results            must always be veriﬁed.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The survey respondents broadly affirm the cluster’s core position: AI use remains subject to independent human verification and personal responsibility, while sanctions are justified for inadequate oversight rather than for AI use itself. Divergent chambers policies—from conditional permission to prohibition—also support the cluster’s account of unresolved AI-specific restrictions.
qs: My one rule is that it is essential that all AI-generated           information be independently veriﬁed.

Sanctioning counsel for ethical lapses is my             least favorite activity as a judge, but I believe that stiﬀ sanctions             are generally appropriate when counsel fails to police their use             of AI adequately.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The survey supports the cluster’s principal proposition through judges’ reports that direct AI use by self-represented litigants can generate plausible but legally erroneous filings, shift substantial screening and verification work onto chambers, and overburden courts. It also aligns with the cluster’s preference for bounded, supervised adoption, although these points are respondent observations and expectations rather than measured causal effects.
qs: My principal concern is that pro se litigants             now regularly use AI to generate lengthy pleadings that look             sophisticated but are often frivolous; this multiplies the amount             of work I and my law clerks have to do in those cases.

And even ordinary pro se litigants who are trying to do the right              thing and who rely on AI may not realize that the brief they had              AI generate that looks pretty good to them is egregiously wrong              about the law.

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s copilot and verification-cost framing. It reports limited-visibility, preliminary uses in judicial chambers and explains that legal-specific grounding can reduce fabricated citations but cannot eliminate substantive errors such as inaccurate summaries of holdings. This reinforces the need for informed human oversight rather than direct reliance on AI output.
qs: Notably, multiple responses state or suggest that the judge does not know whether or how other individuals in their chambers use AI.

For example, “AI for Law” tools provided by legal information providers have access to cases and other resources that allow them to use techniques to mitigate the risks of citing “fake” cases, although it is more diﬃcult to eliminate other types of error (e.g., summarizing the holding of a case).

st.t: Machine judging: Accuracy cannot establish legitimate authority
st.an: The surveyed comments support the cluster’s distinction between bounded AI assistance and judicial authority: respondents require human verification and direct review of litigants’ materials rather than treating improved accuracy as sufficient for autonomous adjudication. Because these are heterogeneous judicial views rather than measured findings or a unified institutional position, they reinforce but do not independently establish the cluster’s broader legitimacy argument.
qs: o AI should always be seen as at most a research aid, and its results            must always be veriﬁed.

And there is no, absolutely no            replacement for reading the materials submitted by the litigants;            AI should never be used or viewed as a shortcut for fulsome            review of the record.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The surveyed judges align with the cluster’s core proposition that AI should augment rather than replace lawyers’ judgment and that outputs require human verification. Their concerns about hallucinated authorities, inadequate oversight, heavy caseloads and possible erosion of legal-analysis skills reinforce the cluster’s account of verification burdens and the need to preserve human capability.
qs: It is not a             substitute, however, for one's own legal research and writing.
I am unlikely             to uncover hallucinated cases and quotes from lawyers’ briefs             and motions unless opposing counsel spots those and brings             those to my attention.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The judges’ varied responses align with the cluster’s central proposition: AI can assist with bounded tasks and improve efficiency while leaving judgment, record review and accountability with humans. They also reinforce that benefits depend on accuracy and effective verification, and that downstream effects may include skill erosion and increased judicial workload rather than straightforward savings or substitution. The survey offers qualitative expectations and anecdotes, not measured staffing or employment outcomes.

kp.k: Survey provides a December 2025 judicial adoption snapshot
kp.d: The authors selected a stratified random sample of 502 bankruptcy, magistrate, district court and court of appeals judges from a population of 1,738. The survey was distributed in December 2025 and closed December 19; 112 judges responded (22.3%), comprising 100 complete responses, eight substantively complete responses and four email responses reporting no work-related AI use. Partial responses were included only for relevant questions. Published as forthcoming in 2026, the findings concern the surveyed federal court categories, not all courts.
qs: We selected a stratified random sample of 502 federal bankruptcy, magistrate, district court, and court of appeals judges from a population of 1,738 current federal judges.
Of the 502 judges that we surveyed via email, 112 responded (22.3% response rate).
Partial responses are only used in the analysis of the relevant questions.

kp.k: AI adoption is widespread but usually infrequent
kp.d: Among 112 respondents to the tool-frequency question, more than 60% reported using a listed AI tool at work, but only 22.4% reported daily or weekly use; 19.6% reported monthly use, 19.6% rare use and 38.4% never using any listed tool. Each judge was classified according to their most frequently used tool. The authors interpret this as adoption that is not yet routinely embedded in most judges' decision-making.
qs: More than 60% of responding judges reported using at least one AI tool in their judicial work.
However, only 22.4% reported using these tools on a weekly or daily basis.
Conversely, 38.4% of judges have never used any of the AI tools listed on the survey in their work.

kp.k: Legal-specific platforms lead reported judicial AI use
kp.d: Respondents reported more frequent use of legal-specific AI than general-purpose tools. Westlaw AI-Assisted or Deep Research led overall reported use at 38.4%, followed by ChatGPT at 28.6%, including rare use. Table 3 reports Westlaw daily use at 5.4% and weekly use at 8.0%, compared with ChatGPT at 0% and 4.5%. No respondents reported using Harvey or Legora. The authors suggest vendor familiarity and perceived reliability may shape adoption; they do not establish those factors causally.
qs: Respondents report more frequent use of legal‑specific AI tools integrated into established research platforms (such as Westlaw’s AI- Assisted Research and similar tools) than of stand‑alone, general‑purpose AI tools such as ChatGPT, Copilot, or Gemini.
This pattern indicates that vendor familiarity and perceived reliability may strongly shape which AI tools judges are willing to deploy in chambers.

kp.k: Research dominates; adjudicative drafting and decision use remain limited
kp.d: Among 110 use-case respondents, 30.0% reported legal research and 15.5% document review; every other individually specified use case was below 10%. Drafting documents not filed in cases was reported by 7.3%, versus 1.8% for filed documents; editing figures were 4.5% and 2.7%, respectively. Only 1.8% reported using AI to make decisions and 4.5% to inform decisions. The broader 10.9% 'decision making' category also includes preparing questions for proceedings and should not be read as the proportion delegating decisions.
qs: The most common AI use case, reported by 30.0% of judges, was to “conduct legal research.”
The other individual use cases were all below 10%, although 13.6% of judges reported using AI for "Other" use cases.
Only 1.8% of judges reported using AI to “make decisions” while 4.5% reported using AI to “inform decisions.”

kp.k: Different survey questions produced inconsistent non-use reports
kp.d: The use-case question elicited approximately 51% reporting no work-related AI use, compared with 38.4% never using listed tools in the frequency question. Fifteen respondents reporting no use nevertheless reported rare (seven), monthly (five) or weekly (three) use of particular tools. The authors suggest omissions or infrequent use may explain the discrepancy, rather than treating either question as an unqualified adoption measure.
qs: The majority of judges (51%) reported, “I don’t use AI in my work.”
The discrepancy may be an unintentional omission or reflect the respondents’ overall infrequent usage of AI tools, or both.

kp.k: Chambers personnel reportedly use AI more than judges
kp.d: Judges reported others in chambers using AI for legal research at 39.8% and document review at 16.7%, compared with their own 30.0% and 15.5%. Approximately 45% reported no AI use by others in chambers, versus 50.9% reporting no personal work use in the use-case question. These are judges' proxy reports, not staff survey responses; some judges expressly did not know whether or how staff used AI. An account of ten fabricated cases among eleven citations is an individual anecdote involving an unidentified platform, not a measured tool error rate.
qs: Similarly, the top AI use case for others working in chambers is also legal research, at 39.8%, followed by reviewing documents at 16.7%.
Notably, multiple responses state or suggest that the judge does not know whether or how other individuals in their chambers use AI.
Judges may not always know how law clerks or staﬀ are using AI, which may lead to under- or over-reporting of AI use by others in chambers.

kp.k: Training availability lags reported willingness to attend
kp.d: Among 108 respondents, 38.9% recalled court administration providing AI training, and 73.8% of that group attended. The findings section reports 61.1% either received no offer or were uncertain; the executive summary separately reports 45.5% no training and 15.7% uncertain. The authors interpret attendance as suggesting unmet demand and recommend making additional training visibly available, rather than establishing demand through a direct measure.
qs: Of the 38.9% of judges who recall AI training being provided by the court administration, a signiﬁcant majority (73.8%) reported attending the training.
This suggests an unmet demand that more AI training should be oﬀered and speciﬁcally in a visible manner.

kp.k: Chambers governance varies and often contains task-specific exceptions
kp.d: Among 108 respondents, 7.4% permitted and encouraged AI, 25.9% permitted it, 20.4% formally prohibited it, 17.6% discouraged but did not formally prohibit it, and 24.1% had no official policy. Qualitative explanations showed exceptions within both permissive and restrictive categories. The authors caution that 'discouraged but not formally prohibited' was ambiguous and describe governance as early-stage, without a dominant approach.
qs: Meanwhile, 24.1% of judges “have no oﬃcial policy” on AI use for those who work in their chambers.
These responses indicate that many judges are not thinking about AI in binary “yes” or “no” terms but instead are evaluating the beneﬁts and risks of speciﬁc AI use cases.
In hindsight, “discouraged but not formally prohibited” is ambiguous.

kp.k: Some judges require verification and preserve human reasoning
kp.d: Individual respondents described AI as an initial research aid subject to independent verification, while retaining human responsibility for reasoning, decisions and writing. Other reported safeguards included source checks, disclosure and permission, restrictions to legal research platforms, and prohibitions on drafting case-related documents. These are reported chambers practices, not uniform judiciary requirements; respondents also raised confidentiality and approved-tool access constraints.
qs: My one rule is that it is essential that all AI-generated information be independently veriﬁed.
I allow AI use, but we speciﬁcally do not allow AI to reason or write for us.
We need an AI tool tailored for the judiciary that does not share information.

kp.k: Personal and professional AI use are statistically associated
kp.d: Among 108 respondents, 11.1% used AI daily outside work and 26.9% weekly; 26.9% rarely used it and 25.9% never did. Comparing personal and professional use, the authors report a chi-squared p-value of 4.30 x 10-6 and Cramér's V of 0.355, interpreted as a moderate association. This finding establishes association, not that personal experimentation causes professional adoption.
qs: A Cramér’s V of 0.355 suggests a moderate strength association between the two variables.
One in ﬁve judges (20.4%) said that they “never” use AI in their personal lives and “never” use AI in their work.

kp.k: Judicial outlook balances potential efficiencies against professional risks
kp.d: The 108 outlook respondents were nearly evenly divided between optimism and concern. Individual judges anticipated resource savings from summarizing records, constructing chronologies, research and administrative assistance, often conditional on accuracy and safeguards. Others feared fabricated authorities, evidence errors, inadequate oversight and erosion of lawyers' and clerks' research, writing and critical-thinking skills. These qualitative comments express perceived benefits, concerns and predictions, not measured productivity gains or demonstrated skill decline.
qs: As shown in Figure 19, there is a nearly even split between judges who are optimistic about AI and those who are concerned.
I believe it will be a signiﬁcant beneﬁt to conserving judicial resources. So long as accuracy can be conﬁrmed.
Concerned that it will degrade lawyers' ability to conduct legal analysis.
Making decisions requires deep thinking and understanding.

kp.k: Unrepresented litigants create both workload concerns and justice opportunities
kp.d: Some respondents reported or anticipated AI-generated, superficially sophisticated but erroneous or frivolous filings increasing chambers workloads. Others identified potential assistance in deciphering handwritten pro se pleadings and urged courts to consider how AI could enhance, or at least not inhibit, access to justice. These are individual judicial observations and recommendations, not quantified findings about unmet legal need or litigation volumes.
qs: My principal concern is that pro se litigants now regularly use AI to generate lengthy pleadings that look sophisticated but are often frivolous; this multiplies the amount of work I and my law clerks have to do in those cases.
It is appropriate to be mindful of the diﬀerent opportunities and risks for unrepresented individuals, and to consider ways that AI can enhance - or at least not inhibit - access to justice.

kp.k: Sampling and measurement limitations constrain generalisation
kp.d: The authors acknowledge self-selection, non-response and social desirability biases despite random selection. They report a hypothetical 95% margin of error of +/- 9.0% for a 50% response proportion among 112 judges, and warn that six appellate responses are not representative. AI was deliberately undefined; omitted tools, ambiguous task categories and proxy reporting could distort estimates. Table 2 reports magistrate and district response rates of 18.1% and 23.6%; the limitations section reverses those percentages. Findings do not extend to state courts or excluded federal court types.
qs: But even with random sampling, self-selection bias, non- response bias, social desirability bias, and other biases can result in unrepresentative survey results.
Estimates for that group should therefore be interpreted as descriptive of the respondents only, and not as representative of all Court of Appeals judges.
We decided not to provide a deﬁnition of artiﬁcial intelligence (AI).
Judges outside the federal judiciary may have a diﬀerent approach to AI use.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The authors find broad but infrequent judicial AI adoption, concentrated in legal-specific research tools rather than routine decision-making.
pts.d: Among 112 responding judges, 61.6% reported at least some use of a listed AI tool, but only 22.4% reported daily or weekly use; 38.4% reported never using any listed tool. Westlaw AI-Assisted or Deep Research was used at any frequency by 38.4%, versus ChatGPT by 28.6%; no respondents reported using Harvey or Legora. The authors interpret the preference for legal-specific tools as potentially reflecting vendor familiarity and perceived reliability, not as proof of those tools' superior accuracy. These are December 2025 self-reports, not longitudinal evidence of adoption growth.

pts.k: AI is primarily supporting research and document work; reported use for drafting filed documents or making decisions is uncommon.
pts.d: The authors report legal research as the leading individual use case for judges (30.0%) and others in chambers (39.8%), followed by document review (15.5% and 16.7%). Judges reported drafting documents not filed in cases at 7.3%, compared with 1.8% for filed documents. Only 1.8% selected making decisions and 4.5% informing decisions. The broader aggregated 'decision making' category of 10.9% also includes preparing questions for proceedings and must not be read as autonomous adjudication. Anonymous respondents commonly describe augmentation: AI provides research starting points or summaries while humans retain responsibility for reasoning, writing, and verification.

pts.k: The authors describe fragmented, early-stage AI governance and infer unmet demand for judiciary-specific training.
pts.d: Among 108 respondents, 33.3% permitted or encouraged chambers AI use, 20.4% formally prohibited it, 17.6% discouraged it without formal prohibition, and 24.1% reported no official policy. Qualitative responses show that these categories often contain task-specific exceptions. On training, 61.1% reported no court-administration training or uncertainty about its availability, while 73.8% of those recalling an offer attended. The authors infer unmet demand from attendance and availability, rather than from a direct measure of demand. Respondents also identify approved-tool access, training, and administrative guidance as constraints on adoption.

pts.k: Personal and professional AI use are associated; one respondent predicts incoming AI-familiar clerks will spread judicial adoption.
pts.d: The authors find a moderate association between judges' personal and professional AI use, reporting chi-square p = 4.30 × 10^-6 and Cramér’s V = 0.355 for 108 respondents. They also describe substantial overlap between judges' own uses and their reports of chambers personnel's uses. Neither result establishes causal direction. Separately, an anonymous somewhat optimistic respondent predicts a 'trickle up' effect as new law clerks arrive; this is an individual forecast, not a survey-tested mechanism.

pts.k: Anonymous judicial respondents report or anticipate time savings, improved research, and conservation of judicial resources, conditional on controlled and reliable use.
pts.d: Respondents identify transcript and exhibit summarization, finding testimony, building chronologies, routine-order templates, and administrative workflow tasks as promising applications. One very optimistic respondent describes closed-universe summarization as already saving substantial time; others forecast benefits without quantified productivity evidence. A somewhat optimistic respondent explicitly expects efficiency without replacement of people or critical thinking. These statements represent individual experiences and expectations, not measured study outcomes or a unified author prediction.

pts.k: Respondents warn that fabricated authorities and facts can contaminate judicial work, making independent verification essential and sometimes deterring adoption.
pts.d: An anonymous judge reports that a clerk's experimental AI memo cited 11 cases, 10 of which were fake; the platform was unknown. Another relays a colleague's experience of a transcript summary inventing a witness. These are anecdotes, not measured model hallucination rates. Some respondents report restricting or abandoning tools because of reliability risks. The authors explain that legal-information providers can use access to source materials to mitigate fabricated-case risks, while errors such as incorrect summaries of holdings remain harder to eliminate. Respondents also anticipate reputational damage and sanctions where human checking fails.

pts.k: Some respondents say AI-generated litigation increases chambers workload and may prolong frivolous proceedings, while others identify potential assistance for unrepresented litigants.
pts.d: A somewhat optimistic respondent reports that lengthy, sophisticated-looking but often frivolous AI-generated pro se pleadings already multiply work for the judge and clerks. A neutral respondent predicts increased motion volume and warns that well-intentioned unrepresented litigants may mistake plausible-looking briefs for correct law. Other respondents suggest AI could help courts decipher or transcribe handwritten pro se submissions. A further respondent calls for attention to AI's opportunities and risks for access to justice; the study does not measure improved access or reduced unmet legal need.

pts.k: Some respondents predict that substituting AI for research, writing, and analysis will erode professional skills and deepen dependence.
pts.d: Neutral, concerned, and very concerned respondents distinguish useful assistance from replacing the intellectual work needed to develop and maintain competence. One connects perceived effects on current undergraduates to the future clerk pipeline, explicitly linking students in 2025 with clerks in 2030. Another asserts long-term intellectual harm through increased reliance on AI. These are concerns and predictions grounded in personal impressions or reported experience, not longitudinal measurements of lawyer or judge performance. The reference to replacing judges is hypothetical, not a finding that replacement is occurring.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is a stratified random-sample survey with a 22.3% response rate; future impacts are largely supported by anonymous qualitative responses rather than outcome tests.
pts.d: The authors sampled 502 judges from a population of 1,738 and received 112 responses: 100 complete, eight substantively complete, and four email-only statements of nonuse. Question denominators vary: tool frequency uses 112 responses, judicial use cases 110, and most remaining questions 108. The authors acknowledge nonresponse, self-selection, social-desirability, undefined-AI, and proxy-reporting limitations. They give an illustrative ±9 percentage-point margin of error at 95% confidence for a 50% response proportion, but separately recognize representativeness risks. Only six appellate judges responded, so those subgroup findings are descriptive rather than representative. The limitations section transposes magistrate and district response-rate percentages; Table 2 and the counts give 18.1% for magistrate judges and 23.6% for district judges. The authors also disclose a measurement discrepancy: 51% selected no work use in the task question, versus 38.4% reporting never using any listed tool. No controlled productivity, legal-quality, workload, or skill-retention study is presented.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Adoption findings describe December 2025; forecasts range from unspecified near-term workflow changes to longer-term professional dependence and the 2030 clerk pipeline.
pts.d: The population was defined using active judges serving as of August 2025, the sample finalized in October, and the survey distributed around December 2 and closed December 19, 2025. The paper is forthcoming in 2026. Claims about future benefits are frequently conditional on reliable outputs, independent human verification, closed-universe or enterprise-only systems, confidentiality, approved access, training, and clear guardrails. Some respondents explicitly defer broader use until reliability improves or administrative guidance arrives. No profession-wide adoption or displacement deadline is supplied.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are federal judges, clerks and chambers staff, court administrators, appearing lawyers, and litigants—especially those without representation.
pts.d: Judges and staff may gain research and administrative assistance but face verification work, erroneous materials, and possible skill erosion. Clerks are described both as potential adoption drivers and as professionals whose training requires independent research and analysis. Court administrators control training, tool access, and aspects of governance. Appearing attorneys face responsibility for accurate submissions and possible sanctions; unrepresented litigants may receive assistance but also produce misleading filings that increase court workload. The sampled courts comprise bankruptcy, magistrate, district including territorial courts, and courts of appeals. The authors do not extend findings to state courts, Supreme Court justices, Court of International Trade judges, or other unsampled federal judges. There are no direct findings about law-firm pricing, staffing structures, ALSP market shares, or lawyer employment displacement.
